title: Remote support tools and techniques
monthTitle: The Helpdesk Professional: ITIL, Ticketing & Soft Skills
summary: Learn how to support users you cannot physically reach, using remote tools safely, securely, and with the consent and trust of the person on the other end.
objectives: Describe the common categories of remote support tools
Always obtain user consent before connecting to their device
Guide a user through actions using clear verbal screen-sharing
Follow security best practices during a remote session
Choose between remote control, screen-share, and remote command tools
Run a safe, professional remote session from start to finish

quiz.q: What must you do before taking remote control of a user's computer?
options: Obtain the user's clear consent and explain what you'll do
quiz.why: Consent is both a courtesy and a security/privacy requirement; you explain what you are doing and the user agrees before you connect.

quiz.q: Which is a key security practice during a remote session?
options: Confirm the user's identity, keep them watching, and end the session cleanly
quiz.why: Verify who you're helping, keep the user present and aware, never ask for passwords aloud, and disconnect cleanly so no access lingers.

quiz.q: When would you guide a user verbally instead of taking remote control?
options: When you can't or shouldn't connect, or to help the user learn
quiz.why: Verbal guidance suits situations where remote tools aren't available or appropriate, sensitive screens are involved, or when teaching the user helps them next time.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid asking a user to read their password to you?
options: It is fine to do so
It is a security risk and against good practice; you should never need their password
quiz.why: Technicians should never collect user passwords; doing so trains users to share credentials and creates a security and accountability risk.

quiz.q: Name two categories of remote support tool and what each is best for.
quiz.answer: Remote-control tools (e.g. for full hands-on troubleshooting), screen-sharing/co-browsing tools (to see what the user sees and guide them), and remote command/management tools (to run scripts or push fixes at scale). Each suits a different level of access and visibility.
quiz.why: Matching the tool to the task keeps sessions efficient and minimises unnecessary access to the user's machine.

quiz.q: Why is ending a remote session cleanly important?
quiz.answer: A clean disconnect ensures no lingering access remains on the user's device, protects their privacy, and confirms to them that you are no longer connected.
quiz.why: Leftover sessions are a security and trust risk; always disconnect and confirm with the user that the session has ended.

body_markdown:
## Supporting people you can't reach

Most support today is **remote**: the user is on another floor, in another city, or working from home. You will rarely walk to the desk. That makes **remote support tools** and the etiquette around them a daily skill. Used well, they let you fix things in minutes that would otherwise take a site visit. Used carelessly, they create security and trust problems.

## The categories of tool

Remote tools fall into a few broad groups:

- **Remote-control tools** let you see *and operate* the user's screen and mouse, as if you were sitting there. Best for hands-on troubleshooting.
- **Screen-sharing / co-browsing** lets you *see* what the user sees while *they* drive. Good for sensitive screens and for teaching.
- **Remote command / management tools** let you run commands or push fixes to many machines at once, often without interrupting the user. Best at scale.

Match the tool to the task: do not take full control when watching the user click would do.

## Consent comes first, always

Before you connect to anyone's machine, **get their consent** and explain what you are about to do. This is both basic courtesy and a privacy/security requirement.

```text
"To fix this fastest, I'd like to connect to your screen remotely.
You'll see a prompt asking you to allow it - I can't connect
unless you accept. You'll be able to see everything I do, and
you can take back control at any time. Is that okay?"
```

Notice it reassures the user they stay in control and can watch. That is how you build trust over a remote link.

## Guiding a user verbally

Sometimes you should *not* connect — the screen has sensitive data, the tool is unavailable, or teaching the user pays off. Then you **guide them verbally**. The skill is giving one clear instruction at a time and confirming each step.

```text
"Let's do this together. Bottom-left, click the Start button -
tell me when you see the menu. ... Great. Now type the word
'control' and press Enter. What do you see now?"
```

Slow, single steps with check-ins prevent the user racing ahead and getting lost.

## Security during the session

A remote session is privileged access, so treat it with care:

- **Verify identity** — confirm you are helping the right person.
- **Never ask for their password** out loud or in chat; you should not need it.
- **Keep the user present and aware** of what you are doing.
- **Avoid opening personal files** or anything unrelated to the issue.
- **End the session cleanly** and confirm the disconnect, so no access lingers.

These habits protect the user, protect you, and keep an auditable, professional standard.

## Your task

Write the spoken script you would use to start a remote-control session with a nervous, non-technical user who is reluctant to let you connect. Include: how you ask for consent, how you reassure them they stay in control, one security point you make, and how you tell them the session has ended at the close. Keep it warm and jargon-free.

slides.narration: Welcome back. These days, most of the people you support won't be sitting next to you. They'll be on another floor, in another city, or working from home. So remote support is a daily skill, and doing it well means more than just knowing the tools. It means consent, security, and trust. In this lesson you'll learn the categories of remote tool and exactly how to run a session that's safe, professional, and reassuring for the user.

But used carelessly, they create real security and trust problems. So we'll focus as much on how you conduct yourself as on which buttons you press.

Screen-sharing lets you see what the user sees while they do the driving, which is great for sensitive screens and for teaching. And remote command tools let you run commands or push fixes to many machines at once, often without interrupting anyone. The skill is matching the tool to the task: don't take full control when just watching them click would do.

It's both basic courtesy and a genuine privacy and security requirement. Look at the script: it explains there'll be a prompt, that you can't connect unless they accept, and crucially that they can see everything and take back control at any time. Reassuring the user they stay in control is exactly how you build trust over a remote link.

Enter. What do you see now?"
slides.narration: Sometimes you shouldn't connect at all. Maybe the screen has sensitive data, maybe the tool isn't available, or maybe teaching the user pays off so they can do it themselves next time. In those cases you guide them verbally. The real skill here is giving one clear instruction at a time, and confirming each step before moving on. Notice in the example how it waits for the user to confirm they see the menu before giving the next instruction. Slow, single steps stop the user racing ahead and getting lost.

slides.title: Security during the session
bullets: Verify you're helping the right person.
Never ask for their password.
Keep the user present and aware.
Don't open unrelated personal files.
slides.narration: A remote session is privileged access, so treat it with real care. First, verify identity, confirm you're actually helping the right person. Second, never ask for their password out loud or in chat, because you should never need it. Third, keep the user present and aware of what you're doing throughout. And fourth, don't go opening personal files or anything unrelated to the issue. These habits protect the user, protect you, and keep an auditable, professional standard for every session.

slides.title: End the session cleanly
bullets: Disconnect fully when done.
Confirm the disconnect with the user.
No lingering access should remain.
It reassures them you've stepped away.
slides.narration: One step beginners often forget: ending the session cleanly. When you're done, disconnect fully and tell the user the session has ended. This matters for two reasons. First, security, you want no lingering access remaining on their device. And second, trust, it visibly reassures the user that you've stepped away and are no longer watching their screen. A leftover, half-open session is both a security risk and a quiet erosion of the trust you worked to build. Always close the loop.

slides.title: Choosing the right approach
bullets: Quick hands-on fix: remote control.
Sensitive screen or teaching: guide verbally.
Many machines at once: remote command.
Least access needed for the job.
slides.narration: Let's bring the choices together. For a quick hands-on fix, remote control is ideal. For a sensitive screen, or when you want the user to learn, guide them verbally instead. And when you need to fix many machines at once, remote command tools are the way. The guiding principle behind all of this is least access: use the minimum level of access needed to do the job. That keeps sessions efficient, respects the user's privacy, and limits risk. It's a habit good technicians carry everywhere.
